transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining we were told you had some, um, spikes in late Feb so want to start there if that's okay, will keep to 45 and then open Qs, alright?
[00:07] Tom Alvarez: yeah thanks Jordan, appreciate it. we saw a big burst during our checkout flow, about 3x normal token volume for ~36 hours, that drove cost up and some latency while our circuit tried to autoscale, so we're trying to figure out if it's on our end or something about the model serving pattern.
[00:20] Maya Patel: got it, thanks Tom. quick clarifying q — was that traffic mostly synchronous low-latency calls or batched background jobs?
[00:26] Hannah Cho: primarily sync, it's the personalization prompt at checkout, can't batch easily, so p95 latency matters to us, like sub 400ms ideally. We saw p95 drift to ~850ms in the peak window.
[00:40] Jordan Lee: okay p95 to 850ms — that's significant. when you say protestize prompt — sorry transcription — personalization prompt length, token lengths? how many tokens on average?
[00:48] Tom Alvarez: approx median 180 tokens, some users 400 tokens; KV cache hit wasn't as effective because prompts vary a lot. also we've got a fair amount of long context for personalization.
[00:58] Maya Patel: That token distribution explains kernel choices — longer sequences push warmups and kv eviction. two immediate levers: prefix caching and request routing to smaller seq-optimized variants; second, quantized model variants or Dedicated where you get predictable throughput.
[01:15] Priya Singh: from finance, curious on ballpark — if we do Dedicated res or Private, what's the econ delta vs hosted? we have a worrisome monthly overrun now.
[01:25] Jordan Lee: short answer — Dedicated gives you committed capacity which reduces per-token unit cost significantly at steady state but requires a commit; Private has higher fixed fees for the infra and on-prem ops but gives you data residency and control. Hosted is simplest but less predictable under spikes. We'll send detailed scenarios.
[01:41] Liam O'Reilly: network note — for Private/VPC we have mandatory egress restrictions and we use an internal HSM for keys, so integration complexity matters. how mature is Redwood's KMS integration?
[01:51] Maya Patel: we integrate with common KMS providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp Vault). On-prem HSMs are supported in Private with a customer-managed connector; it's an extra step but we have runbooks. we'll share the checklist.
[02:05] Tom Alvarez: also security — we need SOC2 and audit logs retention for 2 years for certain transactions. do you guys keep token-level audit logs?
[02:13] Jordan Lee: yes we provide audit logs and can configure retention windows as an add-on; SOC2 attestation available — I'll attach the report. note that full token retention is an opt-in and has cost.
[02:24] Hannah Cho: ok that helps. On the perf side, can you explain how Redwood's autoscaling handled the spike — there was a fallback to a smaller model but that increased hallucinations for some cases and product flipped on us?
[02:36] Maya Patel: right — smart routing will fallback to compatible variants based on policy, but quality regressions are possible. Suggested pattern: canary routes and A/B test prior to full fallback, plus local eval sets to detect quality drift and trigger fallback only for safe paths.
[02:51] Tom Alvarez: we saw a few hallucinations, yeah. Quality regression alerting — is that tied to prompt sets or traffic slices?
[02:58] Jordan Lee: both — Redwood Optimize can monitor evals against a prompt set and flag regressions by route or model. you can tie alerts to a canary rollout.
[03:07] Priya Singh: can we get an ROI calc? if we reduce p95 from 850ms to 300ms by Dedicated, what's the likely cost movement and how long to break even?
[03:17] Jordan Lee: we can build that with your traffic profile — rough rule: Dedicated reduces per-inference cost by ~25-45% depending on utilization. If you're above ~60% utilization of reserved capacity, Dedicated often wins. We'll run scenarios with your percentiles.
[03:31] Hannah Cho: utilization is tricky because of spikes, hence we were considering hybrid — keep core hosted but burst to Dedicated. is that supported?
[03:38] Maya Patel: yes hybrid routing exists — policy-based routing can prefer Dedicated for latency-sensitive routes and fall back to hosted for overflow or non-critical routes. There's also burst capacity options.
[03:49] Liam O'Reilly: what's the SLO guarantee for Dedicated? we need uptime and cold start behavior spelled out for our SREs.
[03:56] Jordan Lee: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and tail-latency targets in the contract. Cold start is minimized with pinned warm pools and we can configure min replicas during traffic windows. We'll include sample SLA language.
[04:08] Tom Alvarez: timeline — we're in a budgeting cycle; decision needed by end of March. can you get pricing and pilot plan in next 4 business days?
[04:15] Jordan Lee: yes we'll aim for that.
[04:18] Maya Patel: for the benchmark — we recommend you send a 24-72 hour production-like sample plus a representative prompt corpus. we'll run p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1M tokens across hosted, dedicated, and quantized variants.
[04:33] Hannah Cho: quick Q on quantization — does Redwood do 4-bit quant or int8? are there quality regressions?
[04:39] Maya Patel: we support several quant profiles; 4-bit and int8 depending on model family. quality varies — some workloads tolerate quant well, others not. part of the bench is to test quant + caching to see unit cost tradeoffs.
[04:52] Tom Alvarez: also curious about rollout automation; we run daily model updates from our training pipeline. can Redwood pin versions and do canary rollouts without us handling infra?
[05:01] Jordan Lee: yes model version pinning and rollout policies are first-class — canary, A/B, auto rollback on quality regressions. we can integrate with your CI via our deploy APIs.
[05:12] Priya Singh: any mention of competitors? we did PoCs with MajorCloudAI and InferX — they were cheaper on raw per-token but worse on latency and ops tooling.
[05:22] Jordan Lee: makes sense — we'll highlight where Redwood's cost/latency/op controls differ.
[05:26] Liam O'Reilly: one last SRE note — we need tracing hooks and per-request ids routed into our observability stack. supported?
[05:34] Maya Patel: yes, request-level tracing and headers pass-through supported, plus sample telemetry integrations we can share.
[05:41] Tom Alvarez: alright good. recap and next steps?
[05:44] Jordan Lee: recap: Jordan to send pricing tiers + SOC2 + sample SLA language; Maya to schedule benchmarks after Hannah shares traffic sample; Hannah to send production-like traffic; Priya to confirm budget date; Liam to share KMS/HSM vendor list and network constraints. We'll aim to close pilot decision by end of month.
[05:58] Priya Singh: thanks everyone, appreciate it.
[06:00] Jordan Lee: thanks — we'll follow up via email with attachments. bye.
